column2: Definite IE (modified Duke): 2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor. Three minor criteria give only 'possible' endocarditis.
Subacute IE on a prolapsing mitral valve after dental work is most likely viridans streptococci from the mouth; benzylpenicillin-based treatment.
Rheumatic fever: eradicate group A strep with penicillin/amoxicillin; with penicillin anaphylaxis use a macrolide (clarithromycin/azithromycin).
IE in people who inject drugs is usually tricuspid (murmur louder on inspiration) and embolises to the lungs as septic pulmonary emboli.
Cardiobacterium hominis is a HACEK organism, often beta-lactamase-producing: switch to ceftriaxone for 4 weeks (6 for prosthetic valves).
Line-associated healthcare IE is most often S. aureus; remove the line, take cultures and give vancomycin until MRSA is excluded.
Sterile vegetations on both sides of the mitral leaflets are Libman–Sacks endocarditis of SLE (malar rash, non-erosive arthritis), especially with antiphospholipid antibodies.
IE after a urological procedure with a non-haemolytic, PYR-positive Gram-positive coccus is Enterococcus faecalis: amoxicillin plus ceftriaxone or gentamicin ~6 weeks.
Migratory arthritis, carditis, nodules and erythema marginatum meet Jones criteria, which also need evidence of recent strep infection: a raised ASO (or anti-DNase B) titre.
A prolonged PR is a Jones (rheumatic fever) criterion, not a Duke criterion; in IE new conduction block may signal an aortic root abscess.
A prosthetic valve is highest risk: ESC/AHA advise single-dose oral amoxicillin 2 g 30–60 min before extraction. NICE advises against routine prophylaxis.
Streptococcus gallolyticus (S. bovis) IE is strongly linked to colorectal neoplasia, so isolating it should prompt colonoscopy.
Late prosthetic valve IE (> 1 year) resembles native IE; an acute illness after a furuncle points to S. aureus, which usually needs rifampicin and early surgery.
New hypertension work-up: U&E/eGFR, urine ACR and dipstick, HbA1c, lipids, ECG and fundoscopy. CT aortography is only for a specific clue.
ESH/ESC grades: 1 = 140–159/90–99, 2 = 160–179/100–109, 3 = ≥ 180/≥ 110 mmHg; 165/105 is grade 2. Confirm with ABPM/HBPM.
First-line: ACEi/ARB, dihydropyridine CCB or thiazide-like diuretic. Beta-blockers are used only for compelling indications (angina, MI, HFrEF, AF).
Addison's disease causes salt loss and hypotension. Conn's, acromegaly and 11β/17α-hydroxylase CAH cause hypertension.
A creatinine rise < 30% (eGFR fall < 25%) with K⁺ < 6 after an ACE inhibitor is expected; continue the drug and monitor.
Severe hypertension with papilloedema (acute organ damage) is a hypertensive emergency (malignant hypertension): admit for controlled IV treatment.
Hypertensive emergency needs a titratable IV drug (labetalol, nicardipine or nitroprusside); lower MAP by ≤ 20–25% over the first hours.
Systemic hypertension makes the aortic valve close forcefully, giving a loud A2. Aortic regurgitation softens A2.
Renal disease (parenchymal and renovascular) is the commonest secondary cause; primary aldosteronism is the commonest endocrine cause.
Apparent resistant hypertension is most often non-adherence (pseudo-resistance); exclude it, white-coat effect and NSAIDs before seeking secondary causes.
Systolic BP rises throughout life; diastolic plateaus or falls after 50–60 as arteries stiffen, hence isolated systolic hypertension in the elderly.
Heart disease (CHD, LVH, heart failure) is the commonest cause of death in hypertension; stroke is most tightly linked to BP level.
Resistant hypertension with hypokalaemia and alkalosis despite an ACE inhibitor suggests primary aldosteronism (Conn's); check aldosterone:renin ratio.
Screen for primary aldosteronism with the aldosterone:renin ratio (correct K⁺ first); confirm by suppression test, then adrenal CT and venous sampling.
Malignant hypertension with encephalopathy and AKI: IV labetalol infusion, lowering MAP by no more than 20–25% in the first hour.
Albuminuria reflects generalised endothelial dysfunction and predicts CV events years ahead; hence urine ACR in the hypertension work-up.
Early renal artery stenosis raises renin (renin-dependent hypertension); a significant stenosis increases peak Doppler velocity.
Thiazides cause hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, gout and hyperglycaemia. Ankle swelling is from dihydropyridine CCBs, not ACE inhibitors.
Grade 3 hypertension with LVH and grade 2 retinopathy but no acute features: start oral treatment now and review within days.
In type 2 diabetes NICE starts an ACE inhibitor at any age (ARB if Black or ACEi-intolerant); add CCB or thiazide-like diuretic next.
Hypertensive urgency (no acute organ damage) is lowered gradually with oral drugs; rapid ED reduction risks stroke and ischaemia.
About 90–95% of hypertension is primary (essential) with no single cause; secondary causes make up only 5–10%.
Keith–Wagener: 1 narrowing/silver wiring, 2 AV nipping, 3 flame haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots, 4 papilloedema.
Hypertensive emergency with asthma: avoid labetalol; use a nitroprusside (or nicardipine) infusion, lowering MAP ≤ 25% in the first hour.
Before calling hypertension resistant, exclude non-adherence (pill count, drug levels) and confirm with ABPM; then seek secondary causes.
In diabetes with confirmed hypertension, start an ACE inhibitor alongside lifestyle advice (reduces albuminuria and nephropathy).
Daytime ABPM 138/85 is above the < 135/85 target on maximum ACEi: step 2 adds a CCB or thiazide-like diuretic (indapamide).
Gestational hypertension is new BP ≥ 140/90 after 20 weeks without proteinuria; proteinuria makes it pre-eclampsia. Labetalol is first line.
Warfarin is an anticoagulant (vitamin K epoxide reductase; factors II, VII, IX, X). Aspirin, clopidogrel and dipyridamole are antiplatelets.
Digoxin is renally excreted, so hepatic impairment matters little. Renal impairment, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypercalcaemia and amiodarone/verapamil precipitate toxicity.
Clopidogrel is a prodrug (CYP2C19) that irreversibly blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor. Omeprazole may reduce its activation; prefer lansoprazole.
Loop diuretics block the Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ co-transporter in the thick ascending limb, the most potent diuresis; they cause hypokalaemia and alkalosis.
